background.definition: Dehydration is a state of negative total body water due to loss of body water with or without salt loss, diminished water intake, or a combination of both.

list.listitem: In a study of nursing home patients admitted to the hospital with acute illness, 34% were diagnosed with dehydration.
In another study, 23% of the patients older than 70 years admitted to the hospital were determined to be dehydrated.
In 1991, Medicare reimbursed over 446 million dollars for hospitalizations with dehydration as the principle diagnosis.

Dehydration (as identified by both prerenal azotemia and orthostasis on admission) was associated with an increased length of stay (13.6 days vs 7.2 days) among 36 patients admitted to an inpatient rehabilitation center.
GI loss: gastroenteritis with diarrhea or vomiting is the most common GI cause of dehydration and hypernatremia, specifically osmotic diarrhea.
Insensible and sweat losses: high environmental heat, exercise, or infection.
Diabetes: osmotic diuresis due to glucose.
Diabetes insipidus: loss of dilute urine either due to decreased antidiuretic hormone (ADH) or resistance to ADH in renal tubules.
Attenuation of thirst/inability to drink water: elderly are at increased risk, as are patients with cognitive impairment, reduced access to water or hypothalamic lesions affecting thirst.
Obesity modifies the association between water intake and hydration status.

In hypertonic dehydration (hypernatremic dehydration) there is depletion of more water than sodium. Causes include overuse of diuretics, infections, fever, or diabetes insipidus. Circulation is not affected unless the loss is large.

In isotonic dehydration there is proportionately equal loss of sodium and water. Causes include diarrheal illness, vomiting and osmotic diuresis of glucose. The clinical manifestations of isotonic dehydration depend on the absolute volume deficit, the rate at which fluid is lost, and the age of the patient.
In hypotonic dehydration, there is depletion of more sodium than water resulting in extracellular fluid (ECF) volume depletion. Causes include overuse of diuretics or salt wasting renal disease.

In disease states, dehydration causes a marked decrease in ECF volume, because water is lost from both the intracellular and ECF compartments. But loss of sodium in stools, urine, or sweat decreases ECF volume markedly and eventually leads to shock. The immediate compensations in shock operate principally to maintain intravascular volume, but they also affect sodium balance.

Patients with vomiting, diarrhea or fever may hydrate with oral fluids prophylactically. However, there is no evidence to support increased fluid intake for respiratory infections. B
Verbal prompts may increase fluid intake in nursing home residents, but environmental and behavioral interventions have uncertain benefits in improving fluid intake among adults with dementia. B

The American College of Sports Medicine has evidence-based recommendations for athletes to prevent dehydration and hyponatremia. Athletes should learn how to recognize dehydration (ie, urine color darker than pale yellow) and individualize their rehydration during and after activity to their losses. Replacing with 500 mL every 20 to 30 minutes four times is better than a single 2 L bolus. C

There is insufficient evidence about health effects of electric fan use during heatwaves. A fan might help to reduce heat loss if the temperature is below 35 deg C but when temparatures are above 35 deg C the fan might actually contribute to heat gain. C
Identify patients at risk for dehydration based on their medical history. C
Most of the classical signs of dehydration are irregularly present in elderly patients with hypernatremia. B
Suspect dehydration in adults with dry mucous membrane, dry axilla, sunken eyes, postural systolic blood pressure decline more than 20 mm Hg, and postural pulse increment more than 30 bpm. C

list.listitem: Criteria for clinical diagnosis of dehydration: Suspicion of increased output and/or decreased intake. At least 2 physiological or functional signs or symptoms of dehydration (eg, dizziness, functional decline, dry mucous membranes). BUN/creatinine ratio more than 25:1 or orthostatic hypotension or pulse more than 100 or pulse change of more than 10 to 20 beats per minute above baseline with change in position.
Clinical signs and symptoms of dehydration generally have low sensitivity and specificity.

Most of the classical signs of dehydration are irregularly present in elderly patients with hypernatremia.
Mild dehydration: some deficits or abnormalities in laboratory values exist, but they do not seriously impair the patient's circulation, organ function, or level of functioning. Examples include: increased thirst in a patient with diarrhea but who is taking oral fluids adequately or a marginally elevated BUN. Generally loss of no more than 5% of body fluid. Signs can include thirst, dry mucous membrane, reduced axillary sweat, reduced urine output, and slight weight loss. Moderate dehydration: Some deficits or laboratory abnormalities exist that impair or are likely to impair circulation or organ functioning but are not immediately life threatening. Examples include: mild increase in confusion or lethargy or decreased blood pressure in a patient with a sodium of 155 mEq/L associated with reduced oral intake. Generally loss of 5 % to 10% of body fluid. Signs include postural systolic blood pressure decline more than 20 mmHg, skin tenting, and sunken eyes. Severe dehydration: abnormalities that are causing significant, life-threatening risks or problems with circulation, organ function or activities of daily living. Examples include: rapidly increasing confusion or lethargy in a patient with a recent illness who is hypotensive or and/or with a serum sodium of 123 mEq/L. Generally associated with more than 10% fluid loss. Signs range from hypotension and pulse increment more than 30 bpm to confusion and shock.

Laboratory tests are useful in diagnosing dehydration and categorizing the type of dehydration. Initial evaluation should include a urinalysis (for color, volume, osmolality), sodium, potassium, chloride, bicarbonate (electrolytes), BUN, creatinine, and calculation of the BUN/creatinine ratio.
Also consider calcium, glucose, hemoglobin, hematocrit, serum osmolality if clinically indicated.

A study in a nursing home suggested that urine color had a good correlation with urine specific gravity and dehydration status in residents with adequate renal function. The correlations were better in females than males.
Refer to for recognizing the type of dehydration based on the result of laboratory testing.
Identify risk factors for dehydration with the medical examination (eg, use of diuretics, dementia, fever, draining wounds).
Evaluate physiological and functional signs and symptoms of dehydration, and confirm the type of dehydration with selective use of laboratory testing ().
Assess the severity of dehydration as mild, moderate, or severe. The type of fluid depends on the type of dehydration and route of administration depends on the severity of dehydration.
See algorithm in for guidance.

Consider using normal saline to treat hypertonic dehydration in a hemodynamically unstable patient and using half normal saline in a hemodynamically stable patient. In hypotonic dehydration, consider using normal saline. In isotonic dehydration, consider half normal saline orally or intravenously. C
The route of administration depends on the severity of dehydration. In mild and moderate dehydration, oral rehydration with electrolyte solution is preferred when feasible. C
Weighing the patient daily may provide the best means of assessing weight gain or loss. C
Hypodermoclysis or subcutaneous infusion of fluids appears as effective as intravenous infusion to treat mild to moderate dehydration among older adults in the nursing home and at home. A
The Holliday-Segar formula for maintenance fluid requirements by weight is 1500 mL + 20 mL/kg for each kg more than 20 kg. C

Treatment depends on the type of dehydration and the severity of dehydration. In general replace one-half of the deficits in the first 24 hours, and the remaining deficits within the next 48 to 72 hours.
Treat hypertonic dehydration (associated with elevated sodium) with normal saline if the patient is hemodynamically unstable and with half normal saline if the patient is hemodynamically stable.
In hypotonic dehydration (associated with low sodium) treat with normal saline.
In isotonic dehydration, half normal saline is given orally or IV for treatment (see algorithm in ).

Route of administration depends on the severity of dehydration. In mild and moderate dehydration, oral rehydration with electrolyte solution is preferred when feasible. Fluids should be given at the rate of 50 to 200 mL/h depending on the hydration status. In severe dehydration, hospitalization and IV fluids are needed.

A systematic review found low-quality evidence that polymer-based oral rehydration solutions resolve acute watery diarrhea about 8 hours faster and reduce the need for intravenous rehydration compared to glucose-based rehydration solutions.
Weighing the patient daily is the best means of assessing weight gain or loss.
Hypodermoclysis (clysis—the SC administration of replacement fluids) is as effective as IV rehydration of older adults with mild to moderate dehydration.
Subcutaneous infusion of fluids provides a better opportunity to treat mild to moderate dehydration in the nursing home and at home.
Patients with severe signs and symptoms such as dizziness, confusion, and lethargy need hospitalization.
Hospitalize hemodynamically unstable patients and those who cannot tolerate oral fluids.
Cerebral pontine myelinolysis: can occur in hypotonic dehydration during rehydration. This should be avoided by correcting serum sodium slowly over a few days (no greater than 1 mEq/h).
Acute renal failure (ARF): replacement of the lost fluids may return the kidney function to normal in prerenal ARF.

In hypovolemic states, the therapeutic goal is to first replenish the intravascular volume with isotonic fluid, either normal saline or Ringer's lactate, administered as a bolus of 1 to 2 L depending on the fluid deficit. Modifications to this is recommended for poor cardiac reserve.
Fluid deficit = [(Serum sodium/140) x Body weight in kg x 0.5] − [Body weight in kg x 0.5].
This formula presumes that the predehydration body weight is known which can be problematic in older patients.
The end point of this fluid resuscitation phase is restoring peripheral perfusion and BP and returning increased heart rate toward normal.
The Holliday-Segar formula for maintenance fluid requirements is 1500 mL + 20 mL/kg for each kg more than 20 kg.

A retrospective review of elderly Medicare beneficiaries hospitalized with dehydration as the principle diagnosis in 1991 showed a 17.4% mortality within 30 days. There was an additional 30.6% mortality in the following 11 months. B

During rehydration, monitor vital signs regularly and check weight daily. Watch for signs of overhydration such as rapid weight gain (>1 lb/d) or progressive edema and signs of volume depletion (reduced skin turgor or fall in BP). C
Repeat laboratories as indicated by the type of dehydration to ensure that fluid electrolyte balance is restored. C

The recommended daily intake of fluids should not be less than 1600 mL/24 h in order to ensure adequate hydration. A fluid intake sheet and urine specific gravity might be the best methods of monitoring daily fluid.
There are insufficient studies to support medically assisted hydration in palliative care patients.

A behavioral intervention consisting of verbal prompts to drink and compliance with patient beverage preferences was associated with increased fluid intake and a decrease in laboratory values indicative of dehydration among a cohort of 63 incontinent nursing home residents.
